J. W. Stanton & Co. 


Vs. 
STEAMSHIP ‘‘ LOUISIANA.’’ 


Answer.—Wm. H. Hunt, Proctor. Filed Jan’y 3d, 1855. 


To the Hon. Theo. H. McCaleb, the judge of the Dist. Court of 
the U. S. in and for the east’n dist. of La., in admiralty sit- 
ting: 

And now Israel C. Harris and H’y Morgan, of New Orleans, 
composing the commercial firm of Harris & Morgan, and Charles 
Morgan, of New York, and Jeremiah Smith, of Galveston, Texas, 
appear before this hon. court, and for answer to the libel and com- 
plaint of J. W. Stanton and William L. Palmer, merchants and 
co-partners under the style of J. W. Stanton & Co., and of Henry 
C. Hopper, all of New Orleans, in the aforesaid district, against 
the steamship ‘‘ Louisiana,’’ her engines, machinery, &c., against 
all persons lawfully intervening for their interest therein, (these 
respondents being the true and lawful owners of said steamship,) 
do allege and propound as follows: 

Ist. That these respondents are ignorant of the matters con- 
tained in the Ist and 4th articles of the said libel; and as to the 
2d, 3d, 5th, and 6th, and the matters therein contained, they be- 
lieve that the same are in a great part falsely alleged, and that 
the truth is as hereafter alleged. 

2d. That on the 22d day of May, A. D. 1855, between the hours 
of 2 and 3 o’clock a. m., the steamship ‘‘ Louisiana’’ was ascend- 
ing the river Mississippi, bound for the port of New Orleans, and 
was then in good order and well and sufficiently equipped and 
manned ; that whilst said steamship was proceeding on her voy- 
age ascending the river, following the east or right bank, and 
keeping as close thereto as it was prudent and usual for vessels to 
keep, and following the proper and customary track of steamships 
ascending the river; and when she had reached a few miles above 
Point a la Hache, and was close to the said eastern bank, in her 
— position, and between the court-house and church on said 

ank, in said river, the officers and oe on duty and on the 
look-out discovered directly above said steamship an object. close to 
the eastern bank presenting the appearance of trees on said bank, 
and instantly afterwards discovered the yards and masts of a ves- 
sel, and then a form of a tow-boat, bearing right down upon them; 
that immediately the signal was given on the ‘‘ Louisiana,’’ by one 
blast of the whistle, that it was her intention to go to the night, 
and that her helm was at once put hard to port, but that said sig- 
nal was not responded to according to the law and usage of the 


* 
** » 


Stanton et al. vs. Harris et al. 


river; that said tow-boat continuing to come on towards said steam- 
ship, the engines of the ‘‘ Louisiana’’ being stopped, the said tow- 
boat and the Louisiana came in collision, the bows of the steam- 
ship running up to the pilot-house of the tow-boat, separating the 
tow-boat fr .-n the ship she had in tow, and causing the said tow- 
boat to sink almost immediately, and before all those on board of 
her had time to escape and be saved, although every effort in the 
power of those on the ‘‘ Louisiana’ was made for their rescue ; 
that the stern of the tow-boat having sunk first, her bows were 
held up by her rigging, which was entangled on the bows of the 
‘¢ Louisiana,’’ and the Louisiana, then lying at right angles with 
the said tow-boat, endeavored to urge said tow-boat nearer to the 
bank, at the request of some of the officers from the tow-boat, but 
that every effort to do so was unavailing, and had only the effect 
of making further inroad into the said tow-boat without moving 
her; that thereupon the engines of the ‘‘ Louisiana’’ were backed, 
and she was disengaged from said tow-boat by cutting loose the 
rigging of the tow-boat, the bows of which thereupon sank ; and 
that thereupon the Louisiana proceeded up the river to her port of 
destination, having on board of her all the officers and those of 
the crew of the said tow-boat (then discovered to be the ‘‘ Anglo 
Celt’’) who had been rescued from the collision. 

3d. That the said ‘‘ Louisiana’’ had on board of her at the time 
of the collision powerful signal-lights, such as are usually carried 
by steamers in the mail service ; that she had a sufficient watch on 
deck and on duty at the time, and was in all respects carefully, 
properly, and skilfully manned and navigated ; but that the said 
tow-boat Anglo-Celt was unskilfully navigated, had no watch or 
an insufficient watch on deck, no proper look-out, and had not the 
customary lights or such as were sufficient to make her course and 

sition visible in time to have prevented the said collision, if it had 

een possible so to do. 

4th. That said collision was in no manner whatever attributable 
to the ‘‘ Louisiana,’’ or to the fault of those on board of her, and 
that everything was done by her tc prevent the same; but that the 
same was caused wholly by the fault, negligence, and want of 
skill of those on board said tow-boat ‘‘ Anglo Celt,’’ by their fail- 
ing to keep burning on her the necessary and usual signal-lights ; 
by their being out of the proper track for vessels descending the 
river at that place; by their failing to give or to answer the sig- 
nals proper for boats meeting one another ; by thei

As soon as animals crept forth on the first lands, a spee- 
chless and degraded crowd, they battled for the acorn and 
or their lairs with claws and fists, then with clubs and at 
length with arms_, which afterwards practice had made; until 
they learned to use words by which to indicate vocal sounds 
and thoughts and to use names. After that they began to 
refrain from war, and fortify walled towns, and to lay down 
laws that no one should be a thief, nor a robber nor an 
adulterer. 

— Horace, Sat., 1. iii. 99. 

Modern science claims to be proving, by the most care- 
ful and exhaustive study of man and his works, that our race 
began its existence on earth at the bottom of the scale, 
instead of at the top, and has been gradually working up- 
ward; that human powers have had a history of development; 
that all the elements of culture — as the arts of life, art, science, 
language, religion, philosophy — have been wrought out by 
slow and painful efforts, in the conflict between the soul and 
the mind of man on the one hand, and external nature on 
the other. 

— Whitney, Oriental and Linguistic Studies, p. 341. 

These communities reflect the spiritual conduct of our 
ancestors thousands of times removed. We have passed 
through the same stages of development, physical and moral, 
and are what we are to-day because they lived, toiled, and 
endeavored. Our wondrous civilization is the result of the 
silent efforts of millions of unknown men, as the chalk cliffs 
of England are formed of the contributions ' of myriads of 
foraminifera. 

— Dr. J. Kaines, Anthropologia, Vol. i, No. 2, p. 233. 




INTRODUCTION 


THREE STAGES OF SOCIAL EVOLUTION 


It is possible for us today to identify three main stages 
of the general evolution of human society. These are the 
primitive pre-class society, class society and the classless 
society taking shape before us over a large area of the world. 
Such a broad division of social evolution is not intended, of 
course, to overlook the fact of uneven development of differ- 
ent peoples. Nor is it meant to ignore the sub-stages of the 
pre-class society and more particularly those of the class 
society. What nevertheless needs to be emphasised is that 
we are liable to miss something of basic significance about 
human history if we do not begin with these three main 
stages of social evolution. 

Notwithstanding the grave anxiety caused these days by 
the development of the thermo-nuclear and biological wea- 
pons of mass destruction, the normal expectation of human 
survival on the earth — and, therefore, also of the classless 
society of the future — is for an immeasurable period of time. 
While looking back at the past, we have a somewhat similar 
impression. The period covered by the primitive pre-class 
society was immeasurably longer than the career of class 
society. On a rough estimate the latter ^*is at best one 
hundredth part of the time during which men have been 
active on our planet.”^ 

In the time-scale, therefore, compared to the primitive 
pre-class society of the past and compared also to the class-

social sciences as well. As Engels very lucidly explained :
